newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Kwasniewski says NATO must be open after expansion.
newsitem.headline: Kwasniewski says NATO must be open after expansion.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, whose country is likely to be among the first new members of NATO, said on Sunday the door should remain open for nations left out of the first wave of alliance enlargement.
He also said he did not expect major new deployments of NATO forces, arguing that a similar effect could be achieved by modernising the Polish army and military infrastructure.

Speaking at a North Atlantic Treaty Organisation security workshop, Kwasniewski said the alliance had to instil a "sense of inclusion" in states which want to join but are not invited after it's summit in Madrid next month.
"Enlargement should be viewed as a single process with more than one stage," Kwasniewski said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said earlier this month that Washington's firm position was that only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic should be invited in the first wave.
But East European analysts have expressed concern that the alliance should remain open to others to prevent any possibility of creating new destablising divisions.
Kwasniewski said the enlargement of NATO was part of the redefinition of its post-Cold War mission, adding: "The alliance's open character is of crucial significance".

The 14th annual workshop, which brings together ministers and top military and political officials, has taken on added significance as a final chance for NATO aspirants to press their case ahead of the Madrid summit.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, who speaks on Monday, is expected to make a final appeal for admission but also lay the ground for a rapid second round of enlargement.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told Clinton at the Group of Seven summit in Denver on Saturday he had made a big mistake by excluding Romania and Slovenia from the first round.
Kwasniewski called on alliance members not to ignore the aspirations of Ukraine to be part of Euro-atlantic structures.
NATO and the former Soviet republic initialled a security pact which will be signed at the Madrid summit.
"The trust which Ukraine places in Western countries and institutions cannot go unanswered," Kwasniewski said.
Opening the workshop, much of it behind closed doors in Prague Castle, Czech President Vaclav Havel urged NATO leaders on Saturday to lay out a clear timetable for expansion beyond the first wave.

"I think it would be excellent...that at the Madrid summit there would be some logic of expansion laid out, and some schedule indicated with an explanation of why or not some countries were taken earlier and whether or not they may be accepted later," he said.
Kwasniewski said the new central European members of the alliance would be fully committed to NATO and were prepared to assume their share of its tasks and responsibilities.

Enlargement, to include states whose forces once faced NATO's as members of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact, will greatly extend the territory under the alliance's security umbrella over the flat plains of central Europe.
